tip: Completed actions mark the doer with ने: मैंने (maine = I). The verb then agrees with the object – निकाले (nikaale) is plural for पैसे (paise = money), not for 'I'.
No ने (ne) here – बचाती है (bachati hai = saves) is a habit, and ने only marks completed past actions. Present-tense doers stay plain: गीता (Geeta), not गीता ने.
Even in the past, ने (ne) skips motion verbs: चली गई (chali gayi = went off) takes no ने. Only verbs that act on an object use it.
You give an exam in Hindi to take it: परीक्षा दी (pariksha di = gave the exam). The examiner is the one who takes it – परीक्षा ली (pariksha li). Reversed from English.
Bills get filled, not paid: बिल भर दिया (bill bhar diya = filled the bill). भरना (bharna = to fill) covers paying bills, fees and fines.
Adding दिया (diya = gave) to a verb means done for someone else: गरम कर दिया (garam kar diya) – heated it for me. With लिया (liya = took) it would be for herself.
Hugging is neck-based: गले लगाया (gale lagaya) is literally 'attached to the neck'. गला (gala) means the neck-throat area – that's where the hug happens.
English words become Hindi verbs through किया (kiya = did): बुक किया (book kiya) = booked. Same pattern for फ़ोन किया (phone kiya) and ऑर्डर किया (order kiya).
